questions.question: What are the basic Git commands a developer needs?
questions.title: Git Basics
questions.direct_answer: Git is version control: it tracks changes to your files over time so you can review history, branch, and collaborate. The core commands: git init (start a repo), git clone URL (copy one), git status (what's changed), git add (stage changes), git commit -m 'msg' (save a snapshot), git push (send commits to the remote), git pull (fetch + merge from remote), git branch (list/create branches), git checkout/switch -b feature (new branch), git merge feature (merge it in), git log (history). The model: working dir -> staging area (add) -> committed history (commit) -> remote (push).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the core loop (status, add, commit, push, pull) and the model (working dir -> staging -> commit -> remote).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Committing without checking git status (staging the wrong files), or not branching for features.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Core loop: status, add, commit, push, pull. Model: working dir -> staging (add) -> commit -> remote (push). Branch per feature; merge to combine.

sections.title: Track Changes Over Time
sections.content: Git is version control: it tracks changes to your files over time so you can review history, branch, and collaborate. The core commands: git init to start a repo, git clone URL to copy one, git status to see what's changed, git add to stage changes, git commit dash m msg to save a snapshot, git push to send commits to the remote, git pull to fetch and merge from the remote, git branch to list or create branches, git checkout or switch dash b feature to make a new branch, git merge feature to merge it in, and git log to see history. The model is working dir to staging area via add to committed history via commit to the remote via push, and a branch per feature keeps main stable.

sections.title: The Git Flow
sections.content:
working dir -> add (staging) -> commit (history) -> push (remote).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  W[working dir] -->|git add| S[staging]
  S -->|git commit| H[local history]
  H -->|git push| R[remote]
  R -->|git pull| H
```

sections.title: The core Git commands
sections.content:
```ruby
# Core loop (do this many times a day):
#   git status                 # what's changed
#   git add .                  # stage all changes (or `git add file.rb`)
#   git commit -m 'fix login bug'  # save a snapshot
#   git push                   # send commits to the remote
#   git pull                   # fetch + merge from remote

# Branching (one branch per feature):
#   git switch -c add-login     # new branch
#   ... work, commit ...
#   git switch main            # go back
#   git merge add-login        # merge the feature in

# History:
#   git log --oneline          # one-line history
#   git diff                   # unstaged changes
#   git diff --staged          # staged changes

# Clone a repo:
#   git clone https://github.com/org/repo.git
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Committing without checking git status — you may stage the wrong files.
Working directly on main instead of branching per feature (hard to review/revert).
git pull without checking for conflicts (use git pull --rebase for a clean history).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Git tracks changes over time; the core loop is status, add, commit, push, pull.
Model: working dir -> staging (add) -> commit (history) -> push (remote).
Branch per feature (git switch -c) so main stays stable and reviewable.
git merge combines a branch; git log shows history.
Always git status before add/commit so you stage the right files.
